newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rise on inflation data, dollar mixed.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rise on inflation data, dollar mixed.

text.p: Stocks and bonds rose while the dollar was mixed on Friday as news of mild inflation eased Wall Street's fears about rising interest rates.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 56.57 points to 6,935.46, recouping about a third of Thursday's 160-point drop sparked by strong February U.S. retail sales data that rekindled fears of inflation and higher interest rates.
The Dow's gains for the day trimmed its loss for the week to 65.43 points.
In the broader market, gainers outpaced losers by 1,408 to 1,028 on volume of 486.9 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The recovery began as early news of a surprisingly big drop in wholesale prices in February helped eased concerns that the Federal Reserve would raise rates in a bid to ward off inflation.

The Producer Price Index fell 0.4 percent in February, a bigger drop than economists had forecast, and the core rate excluding volatile food and energy prices fell 0.1 percent, instead of rising 0.1 percent as expected.
The report cast doubt on forecasts that the Fed, the nation's central bank, will raise rates at its policy-making meeting on March 25.
The inflation-wary bond market welcomed the news. The benchmark 30-year Treasury rose 6/32, or $1.875 on a $1,000 bond, reducing the yield to 6.94 percent from 6.96 percent at Thursday's close.

Despite the report, analysts said the Fed's next move on rates was an open question, noting Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan in recent comments focused on the need to quash future rather than current inflation risks.
But the severity of Thursday's sell-off, analysts said, meant the stock market had room to advance even without a clear green light on the interest rate front.
That sell-off was triggered by an unexpected surge in U.S. retail sales. While the rise suggested a surprisingly robust economy, analysts said the market's reaction was overblown.

"The data we saw yesterday didn't warrant a 160-point drop," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "But a lot of that may have been people anticipating a sloppy PPI and we certainly didn't get that."
With the Fed meeting still more than a week away, analysts said the market was likely to remain volatile.

"Any sign of economic weakness will be taken as a temporary reason to rally," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates. "But it's all going to come down to what happens on the 25th."
In late trading, the dollar fetched 1.6952 German marks, down from 1.7047 marks on Thursday. The dollar edged up to 123.45 Japanese yen from 123.34 yen.
Soybean futures rose as speculators bet that Brazil would slap an export tax on its soybeans.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, May soybeans closed 21 cents a bushel higher at $8.49-1/2 as professional commodity fund investors bought at least 20 million bushels.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil soared as speculators bet on a reversal of recent sharp losses.
April crude oil closed at $21.29 a barrel, up 59 cents.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index ended 26.6 points higher at 4,424.3, up four points from a week earlier. In Japan, the Nikkei 225 average gained 23.16 points to finish at 17,923.64, a fall of 275.10 for the week.
